vignette: Ethan is a nineteen-year-old fast food worker living in a small town on the East Coast. Recently, he has been struggling with lingering effects from a powerful hurricane that hit his area last summer. The storm caused extensive damage to the coastal towns, and Ethan's community wasn't spared. On the day of the disaster, Ethan was working his usual shift at the fast food restaurant where he serves burgers and fries. By mid-afternoon, weather warnings were escalating, and the sky had turned an ominous gray. Despite the worsening conditions, Ethan felt obligated to stay at work until his manager dismissed him around 6 PM. As he rushed home on his scooter, the rain intensified and strong winds began to uproot trees and toss debris through the air. Once home, Ethan tried to stay safe in his basement with a few of his family members. The noise was overwhelming-like a never-ending thunderclap-and the entire structure trembled with each gust of wind. It felt like chaos would soon engulf them all. For hours, he could hear the roar and the crashes of things being torn apart outside, waiting anxiously for any signs that the worst had passed. The next morning, Ethan emerged from his basement to a landscape transformed beyond recognition: uprooted trees, crumbled houses, broken windows everywhere. The sight left him feeling disoriented and profoundly sad about the loss. He spent the days following the disaster helping in community clean-up efforts but found himself frequently overwhelmed by memories of the storm. Now, months later, Ethan still wakes up in a cold sweat from nightmares where he relives the hurricane's fury. These dreams are so vivid that when he wakes up, he sometimes thinks it's happening all over again-feeling his heart race and palms sweating as though he is back on the scooter or hiding in the basement. He avoids watching the weather channel or news reports about storms, but even hearing a distant rumble of thunder can trigger intense anxiety. At work, Ethan often feels like something bad is going to happen again at any moment. Small things that others might not notice-a loud noise outside the restaurant, an unexpected phone call-can startle him and plunge him into a state of high alertness. He sometimes finds it hard to concentrate on his tasks, as intrusive thoughts about the hurricane keep popping up in his mind. Ethan has also noticed changes in how he interacts with people. While previously outgoing and friendly, he now tends to isolate himself more often than not. Social gatherings or crowded places make him uncomfortable; the constant buzz of activity brings back feelings of being trapped and helpless. His relationships have suffered as a result-he's withdrawn from friends who don't understand why he won't go out anymore. Despite these challenges, Ethan tries his best to carry on with daily life. He goes to work because it gives him some structure and routine, but he finds himself frequently distracted or feeling anxious while on the job. His mind often drifts back to that fateful day and the days that followed, replaying those terrifying scenes over and over again. Although Ethan acknowledges these difficulties, he hasn't yet sought professional help for his struggles. He's hoping things will eventually get better on their own, but the lingering effects of that traumatic event continue to affect him deeply and impact nearly every aspect of his life.
